frictionVectors.title: Gas Dependence and Export Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Algeria retains strong state control over hydrocarbons, but European demand, price negotiations, and infrastructure links constrain its strategic autonomy. Declining domestic investment and rising internal consumption add pressure.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Competition for Strategic Minerals
frictionVectors.details: Chinese, European, Turkish, and Gulf actors are competing for access to mining, logistics, and industrial projects. Algiers is seeking technology and capital without surrendering control of strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Chinese Debt and Infrastructure Leverage
frictionVectors.details: Angola is diversifying financing, but past oil-backed obligations and major Chinese-built infrastructure continue to shape fiscal and strategic choices. Debt restructuring has not eliminated external leverage over resource revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Lobito Corridor Strategic Contest
frictionVectors.details: The United States, European partners, and China are competing for influence around the Lobito Corridor and access to critical-mineral supply chains. Angola benefits from the rivalry but must prevent logistics infrastructure from becoming externally dominated.

frictionVectors.title: Cotonou Port and Regional Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Benin is strengthening Cotonou as a logistics and industrial hub, but trade remains vulnerable to relations with Nigeria and external operators. Foreign investment is useful for infrastructure yet limits full national control of transport assets.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence from the Sahel is increasing pressure on northern border communities and transport routes. Security partnerships and surveillance assistance bring outside support while creating dependence on foreign capabilities.

frictionVectors.title: Diamond Market Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Botswana retains unusually strong negotiating power through Debswana and state participation, but fiscal and export exposure to global diamond demand remains substantial. Lab-grown diamonds and weaker luxury consumption threaten the revenue base.

frictionVectors.title: Critical-Mineral Investment Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign investors are seeking access to Botswana's copper, nickel, uranium, and other mineral prospects. Gaborone is pursuing diversification while maintaining regulatory control and avoiding excessive dependence on any single partner.

frictionVectors.title: Gold-Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is seeking greater state participation and tighter oversight of industrial and artisanal gold production, challenging established foreign mining interests. This may increase public capture of revenues but risks reduced investment and opaque governance.

frictionVectors.title: Russian Security Partnership
frictionVectors.details: Ouagadougou is turning toward Russian security support while reducing reliance on France and other Western partners. The arrangement may reinforce regime autonomy, but payments, mining access, and battlefield dependence could create a new form of external leverage.

highlights: Critical-minerals hopes meet weak negotiating power

frictionVectors.title: Mining concessions and informal extraction
frictionVectors.details: Burundi is seeking greater value from nickel, gold, and rare-earth prospects, but limited state capacity and opaque licensing leave room for foreign firms and politically connected intermediaries to capture rents.

frictionVectors.title: Rwanda border and trade tensions
frictionVectors.details: Strained relations with Rwanda complicate cross-border commerce and security coordination, increasing Burundi's dependence on longer routes through Tanzania and the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

highlights: Stable Atlantic gateway with diversified partnerships
Tourism and maritime assets drive leverage

frictionVectors.title: Port and maritime-security competition
frictionVectors.details: Mindelo and other maritime facilities attract European, Chinese, and wider Atlantic interest. Praia must balance investment, naval access, and sovereignty while preventing strategic infrastructure from becoming externally controlled.

frictionVectors.title: Tourism-dependent resource pressure
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-owned tourism and real-estate projects provide revenue but intensify pressure on water, land, and coastal ecosystems, limiting domestic control over key economic assets.

highlights: Oil, gas, timber, and transit assets remain externally contested
Security crises constrain state bargaining power

frictionVectors.title: Resource concessions and infrastructure dependence
frictionVectors.details: Foreign operators and lenders remain central to oil, gas, timber, mining, and major transport projects. Debt, contract opacity, and limited processing capacity reduce Cameroon's ability to retain value domestically.

frictionVectors.title: Anglophone conflict and regional insecurity
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in the Northwest and Southwest disrupts roads, agricultural production, and investment, while instability around the Far North and eastern borders diverts resources from economic sovereignty.

highlights: Mineral wealth remains vulnerable to opaque deals

frictionVectors.title: Russian security and mining influence
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security personnel and political networks retain influence around regime protection and mineral access, limiting Bangui's independent control over gold and diamond revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Corridor insecurity and regional dependence
frictionVectors.details: Poor roads and insecurity along routes to Cameroon and Sudan constrain exports and humanitarian supply. Dependence on external escorts, contractors, and neighboring transit states weakens effective sovereignty.

highlights: Oil revenues underpin a tightly managed transition
Sudan war raises border and corridor risks

frictionVectors.title: Oil-sector concentration and external operators
frictionVectors.details: Chad's fiscal position remains heavily tied to oil produced and marketed through foreign-linked operators and regional infrastructure. Price volatility and limited refining capacity constrain domestic control over the value chain.

frictionVectors.title: Sudan spillover and foreign security ties
frictionVectors.details: The Sudan conflict places pressure on eastern borders, refugee systems, and trade routes while encouraging reliance on external security partners. This reduces policy autonomy during the political transition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and logistics dependence
frictionVectors.details: External financing and management influence around ports, transport, and telecommunications can improve connectivity while limiting domestic control over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: Maritime boundary pressure
frictionVectors.details: The Comoros remains reliant on external partners for maritime surveillance and fisheries protection, leaving its surrounding waters vulnerable to illegal exploitation.

frictionVectors.title: Cobalt and copper leverage
frictionVectors.details: Foreign firms and trading networks retain substantial influence over copper and cobalt value chains, while weak local processing limits the state's ability to capture resource rents.

frictionVectors.title: M23 and regional interference
frictionVectors.details: Conflict in North Kivu and South Kivu continues to undermine state control, with Rwanda-linked allegations, armed-group financing, and competing external security interests complicating sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon concentration
frictionVectors.details: Oil remains the central source of export earnings and public finance, exposing the country to foreign operator influence, price volatility, and limited domestic value addition.

frictionVectors.title: Debt-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-financed roads, ports, and public works deepen connectivity but increase dependence on external contractors, lenders, and commodity-backed repayment structures.

frictionVectors.title: Cocoa value-chain imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Côte d'Ivoire is expanding local processing and seeking stronger producer returns, but multinational buyers and global price-setting mechanisms still capture much of the value.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahel security spillover
frictionVectors.details: Jihadist violence and political instability north of the border are driving higher security costs and dependence on regional and international partners to protect transport corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign military basing
frictionVectors.details: U.S., Chinese, French, Japanese, and other military presences provide revenue and strategic leverage but constrain independent security policymaking and intensify great-power competition.

frictionVectors.title: Port and debt dependence
frictionVectors.details: Djibouti's logistics economy relies heavily on foreign-funded port infrastructure and Ethiopian trade, creating exposure to debt stress, external control, and regional disruption.

frictionVectors.title: GERD and Nile security
frictionVectors.details: Egypt continues to oppose unilateral Ethiopian management of the Grand Ethiopian Renaissance Dam, viewing reduced Nile flows as an existential sovereignty issue. Diplomatic channels remain active but mistrust is entrenched.

frictionVectors.title: External financing dependence
frictionVectors.details: IMF conditions, Gulf investment, and asset sales are stabilizing Egypt’s finances while increasing outside influence over strategic infrastructure and state-linked enterprises.

highlights: China remains a key infrastructure partner

frictionVectors.title: Hydrocarbon depletion
frictionVectors.details: Falling mature-field output is narrowing fiscal space and increasing pressure to attract foreign capital for new offshore development. The state retains formal control but has limited bargaining power.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: Chinese-backed construction and other external partnerships support roads, ports, and urban projects while creating long-term financial and political dependence.

frictionVectors.title: Regional militarization
frictionVectors.details: Eritrea’s position along the Red Sea keeps it strategically relevant to Gulf states and wider maritime competition. Tensions with Ethiopia and instability around the Horn create persistent sovereignty risks.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign mining dependence
frictionVectors.details: Gold and base-metal projects provide revenue but remain reliant on foreign operators, technology, and capital. Limited transparency increases concerns over the distribution of resource gains.

frictionVectors.title: Fiscal dependence
frictionVectors.details: Heavy reliance on Southern African Customs Union receipts and South African supply chains constrains independent economic policy. Revenue volatility exposes the monarchy to external shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Governance and investment tension
frictionVectors.details: Political restrictions and periodic unrest complicate efforts to attract diversified foreign investment. External partners prioritize stability, while domestic groups demand broader political and economic participation.

frictionVectors.title: Nile and port access disputes
frictionVectors.details: The GERD expands Ethiopia’s electricity leverage but continues to generate acute tensions with Egypt and Sudan. Dependence on Djibouti and contested arrangements for alternative maritime access remain strategic vulnerabilities.

frictionVectors.title: External financing and conflict
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and reliance on international lenders limit policy autonomy, while violence in Amhara and Oromia undermines infrastructure security and investor confidence.

highlights: Manganese and oil anchor the economy

frictionVectors.title: Foreign control of extractives
frictionVectors.details: The government is seeking greater local processing and fiscal returns from oil, manganese, and timber, but foreign firms still dominate capital, technology, and export channels.

frictionVectors.title: Railway and port dependence
frictionVectors.details: Manganese and other mineral exports remain dependent on aging rail and port infrastructure, leaving Gabon exposed to external operators, financiers, and logistics bottlenecks.

frictionVectors.title: Fishing access and maritime control
frictionVectors.details: Foreign fishing fleets and limited enforcement constrain The Gambia's ability to capture the full value of its coastal resources and protect small-scale fishing communities.

frictionVectors.title: Senegal-linked infrastructure exposure
frictionVectors.details: The country's trade routes, energy links, and land access are heavily tied to Senegal, creating practical leverage over Banjul despite generally cooperative bilateral relations.

frictionVectors.title: Illegal mining and environmental loss
frictionVectors.details: Illegal gold mining continues to damage water systems and undermine state authority, with networks involving local elites, financiers, and foreign-linked traders.

frictionVectors.title: IMF and mining-investor constraints
frictionVectors.details: Debt restructuring and IMF-backed fiscal discipline limit policy space as Accra seeks higher royalties, domestic processing, and stronger bargaining power with multinational miners.

frictionVectors.title: Simandou consortium dependence
frictionVectors.details: The iron-ore project promises transformative revenue but relies on foreign mining capital, Chinese-linked infrastructure, and complex rail-and-port arrangements that dilute immediate sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Bauxite value-chain imbalance
frictionVectors.details: Guinea remains a major bauxite exporter while refining and downstream industries lag, leaving the state vulnerable to external buyers and volatile commodity demand.

highlights: State capacity is the binding constraint

frictionVectors.title: Cashew export dependence
frictionVectors.details: Unprocessed cashew exports leave farmers and the state dependent on foreign buyers, seasonal trading networks, and external price formation.

frictionVectors.title: Political instability and illicit routes
frictionVectors.details: Repeated institutional crises weaken customs and maritime enforcement, creating openings for narcotics trafficking, opaque commercial networks, and outside influence over strategic assets.

frictionVectors.title: External Debt and Strategic Rail
frictionVectors.details: Debt servicing and foreign-financed rail infrastructure continue to limit Nairobi's fiscal room and bargaining power over major transport assets. Kenya is seeking to diversify financing while preserving control of the Mombasa-Nairobi corridor.

frictionVectors.title: Lamu Corridor Security
frictionVectors.details: The Lamu port and associated corridors face security and commercial risks linked to regional instability and militant activity from Somalia. Delays in corridor development weaken Kenya's ability to capture regional transit value.

frictionVectors.title: Highlands Water Project
frictionVectors.details: Lesotho's water exports provide strategic revenue but deepen dependence on South Africa, which remains the dominant buyer and infrastructure partner. Project financing, compensation, and local benefit-sharing remain politically sensitive.

frictionVectors.title: Infrastructure and Political Volatility
frictionVectors.details: Reliance on external contractors and South African-linked infrastructure limits domestic control over strategic assets. Political instability can delay project execution and reduce negotiating leverage.

frictionVectors.title: Iron Ore Concessions
frictionVectors.details: Foreign mining operators dominate capital-intensive iron ore development, rail access, and export logistics. Liberia retains formal sovereignty but faces persistent pressure to balance investor stability with local employment, taxation, and community benefits.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Corridor Control
frictionVectors.details: Control of Buchanan and other transport corridors is closely tied to mining concessions and external investment. Weak domestic infrastructure leaves Monrovia reliant on foreign capital for strategic logistics.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of Security Space
frictionVectors.details: Competing foreign ties involving Turkey, Russia, Egypt, and Gulf actors continue to shape Libya's military balance and political bargaining. External security support constrains national control over ports, airfields, and energy infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Oil Institution Rivalry
frictionVectors.details: Political fragmentation periodically threatens production, export terminals, and the distribution of oil revenues. International buyers and foreign operators remain central to maintaining output while domestic authorities contest control of the sector.

frictionVectors.title: Nickel and Cobalt Exposure
frictionVectors.details: Large mining projects depend heavily on foreign capital, technology, and export markets, limiting Madagascar's ability to capture value beyond royalties and employment. Commodity-price volatility creates fiscal and political vulnerability.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Communities and Land Rights
frictionVectors.details: Foreign-linked mining and mineral exploration generate recurring disputes over land access, environmental damage, and compensation. Weak state capacity makes enforcement of local benefit-sharing commitments inconsistent.

frictionVectors.title: Mining Concession Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Malawi is seeking uranium, rare-earth and graphite investment to diversify exports, but weak bargaining power and financing needs could leave the state with limited value capture.

frictionVectors.title: Debt and Import Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: External debt restructuring and foreign-exchange shortages constrain policy autonomy, while reliance on imported fuel, fertilizer and food exposes the country to external shocks.

frictionVectors.title: Gold Sector Renegotiation
frictionVectors.details: The junta is asserting greater state control over gold through revised mining rules and audits, increasing tensions with foreign operators while operational uncertainty and insecurity remain high.

frictionVectors.title: Sahel Security and Logistics
frictionVectors.details: Russian-linked security support has replaced much Western cooperation but has not resolved insurgency risks, threatening transport corridors, mining sites and regional trade.

frictionVectors.title: GTA Gas Dependence
frictionVectors.details: The Greater Tortue Ahmeyim project offers new export revenue and regional leverage, but reliance on foreign operators, offshore infrastructure and Senegalese coordination limits immediate sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Mining and Port Concentration
frictionVectors.details: Iron-ore exports remain concentrated in the state-linked SNIM system and the Nouadhibou corridor, leaving revenues exposed to commodity prices and external infrastructure financing.

frictionVectors.title: Chagos Strategic Bargaining
frictionVectors.details: Mauritius is pursuing sovereignty over the Chagos Archipelago while negotiating the future of the strategically important Diego Garcia base with the United Kingdom and United States.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Maritime Competition
frictionVectors.details: Port Louis seeks greater Indian Ocean logistics and blue-economy capacity, balancing Indian, Chinese and Western commercial and security interests without losing regulatory autonomy.

frictionVectors.title: Western Sahara Resource Legitimacy
frictionVectors.details: Morocco is expanding phosphate, fisheries, renewable-energy and port projects in Western Sahara, drawing diplomatic and legal opposition from the Polisario Front and its supporters.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital Balancing
frictionVectors.details: Large-scale infrastructure and green-energy projects attract European, Gulf, Chinese and U.S. partners; Rabat retains strategic leverage but remains exposed to external technology, finance and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Security and LNG Access
frictionVectors.details: International energy companies and security partners remain central to protecting offshore gas investments and reopening northern projects. This limits Maputo's effective control over the security conditions surrounding its largest prospective export sector.

frictionVectors.title: Cabo Delgado Insurgency
frictionVectors.details: Insurgent attacks and weak state presence continue to disrupt communities, logistics, and resource development. Regional and external military support reduces immediate pressure but does not resolve local grievances.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Control of New Energy Assets
frictionVectors.details: Oil, uranium, green hydrogen, and critical-mineral projects attract major foreign capital and technology. Namibia is seeking local-content and state-participation rules to prevent strategic assets from becoming externally controlled enclaves.

frictionVectors.title: Water and Power Constraints
frictionVectors.details: Large hydrogen and mining projects face limited water, transmission, and port capacity. Infrastructure dependence could give foreign developers and financiers disproportionate influence over national planning.

frictionVectors.title: Pipeline and Oil Export Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Niger's access to coastal export infrastructure remains vulnerable to political disputes and regional insecurity. Reliance on cross-border corridors constrains the junta's ability to convert resource nationalism into dependable revenue.

frictionVectors.title: External Security Realignment
frictionVectors.details: The withdrawal of Western forces and deeper Russian security ties have increased Niamey's room to reject former partners. The shift also raises risks of sanctions, reduced technical support, and weaker oversight of extractive projects.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign Capital and Oil Governance
frictionVectors.details: International oil firms remain important to offshore production, technology, and financing, while Nigeria struggles to capture more value from declining output. Contract uncertainty, theft, and regulatory weakness dilute sovereign control.

frictionVectors.title: Power, Pipeline, and Refining Gaps
frictionVectors.details: Unreliable electricity, damaged pipelines, and weak gas-processing infrastructure limit industrial sovereignty. New domestic refining capacity improves leverage, but imported equipment, finance, and feedstock constraints remain significant.

frictionVectors.title: Eastern Congo Mineral Supply Chains
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's security posture in eastern Democratic Republic of the Congo is closely tied to regional trade and contested mineral flows. International scrutiny and sanctions pressure threaten Kigali's diplomatic and commercial access.

frictionVectors.title: External Finance Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Rwanda's development model relies heavily on foreign aid, investment, and concessional finance alongside state-led mineral processing. This supports infrastructure expansion but leaves policy space exposed to donor and lender conditions.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Licensing Uncertainty
frictionVectors.details: São Tomé and Príncipe is balancing prospective offshore hydrocarbons with environmental concerns, limited state capacity, and dependence on external investors. Uncommercial discoveries or opaque concessions could constrain future resource sovereignty.

frictionVectors.title: Gulf of Guinea Maritime Exposure
frictionVectors.details: The country relies on foreign partners for maritime surveillance and fisheries enforcement. This improves security but leaves control over its waters dependent on outside finance, technology, and naval cooperation.

highlights: New oil and gas era begins

frictionVectors.title: Contract Renegotiation Pressure
frictionVectors.details: Dakar is seeking greater state participation and revised terms in major offshore projects while preserving investor confidence. Disputes with international operators could delay production or raise financing costs.

frictionVectors.title: Offshore Fisheries Competition
frictionVectors.details: Industrial fleets and foreign fishing access continue to pressure coastal communities and artisanal fishers. New hydrocarbon activity adds concerns over exclusion zones, environmental damage, and the distribution of maritime revenues.

frictionVectors.title: Tuna Access and Fisheries Control
frictionVectors.details: Seychelles benefits from tuna-related activity but remains exposed to unequal bargaining with distant-water fleets and foreign fishing interests. Stronger monitoring is needed to convert maritime assets into durable national revenue.

frictionVectors.title: Strategic Maritime Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Indian, European, and other partners support surveillance, port access, and maritime security. These arrangements enhance capacity while creating sensitivity over the country's strategic alignment and control of critical maritime infrastructure.

frictionVectors.title: Large-Scale Mining Bargains
frictionVectors.details: Iron ore, rutile, and emerging critical-mineral projects attract foreign capital but generate persistent disputes over royalties, land, environmental standards, and local employment. Weak enforcement can leave the state bearing social and ecological costs.

frictionVectors.title: Port and Export Infrastructure Dependence
frictionVectors.details: Mining and agricultural exports depend on externally financed ports, roads, rail links, and energy systems. Infrastructure deals can improve connectivity while narrowing government leverage over strategic logistics corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Federal Hydrocarbon Authority Dispute
frictionVectors.details: Mogadishu's offshore licensing ambitions face competing claims from federal member states and disputed jurisdictions. International operators and security partners may gain leverage before Somalia develops a fully unified regulatory and revenue-sharing system.

frictionVectors.title: Red Sea Port Competition
frictionVectors.details: Turkey, the Gulf states, Ethiopia, and other actors are competing for influence over Somali ports, maritime security, and logistics routes. External infrastructure and security agreements risk deepening federal-regional tensions and diluting national control.

frictionVectors.title: Mineral-processing dependence
frictionVectors.details: South Africa retains substantial mineral assets but remains exposed to foreign capital, export-market pressure, and limited domestic refining capacity, particularly for platinum-group metals and battery minerals.

frictionVectors.title: Grid and freight bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity reliability and rail-port congestion continue to reduce sovereign control over industrial supply chains and increase dependence on private and external infrastructure solutions.

highlights: Oil revenues remain the state’s lifeline

frictionVectors.title: Oil corridor vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: South Sudan depends on export infrastructure crossing Sudan, leaving its fiscal base exposed to war, pipeline disruption, and external leverage over transit arrangements.

frictionVectors.title: Elite and foreign resource capture
frictionVectors.details: Weak institutions, armed networks, and opaque contracting limit public control over oil revenues while foreign commercial and security interests compete for access.

highlights: Gold remains a central conflict economy

frictionVectors.title: Gold-for-arms networks
frictionVectors.details: Competing military authorities and external intermediaries use gold production and export channels to finance operations, weakening civilian oversight and national revenue capture.

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor contestation
frictionVectors.details: Control of Port Sudan, oil infrastructure, and Red Sea access carries major strategic value, drawing regional competition and exposing trade routes to military disruption.

highlights: Ports and critical minerals gain strategic weight

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-led infrastructure leverage
frictionVectors.details: Rail, port, and energy projects bring capital and connectivity but can create long-term dependence on external financiers, operators, and strategic partners.

frictionVectors.title: Mining sovereignty tensions
frictionVectors.details: The government is strengthening local-beneficiation and revenue rules, yet disputes over contracts, licensing, and foreign ownership remain politically sensitive.

highlights: Lomé remains a regional trade gateway

frictionVectors.title: Port and corridor dependence
frictionVectors.details: Lomé’s importance as a Gulf of Guinea logistics hub creates exposure to foreign shipping, financing, and security interests while linking Togo’s economy to unstable Sahelian corridors.

frictionVectors.title: Phosphate-sector control
frictionVectors.details: Phosphates remain a strategic national asset, but production and infrastructure constraints limit value capture and sustain reliance on external technology and markets.

frictionVectors.title: EU Migration and Financing Leverage
frictionVectors.details: European financing and migration cooperation remain closely linked, giving external partners influence over Tunisia's policy space. Domestic resistance to perceived conditionality limits deeper alignment.

frictionVectors.title: Energy Import Exposure
frictionVectors.details: High dependence on imported hydrocarbons and constrained investment in renewables leave Tunisia vulnerable to price shocks and external supply conditions.

frictionVectors.title: EACOP Financing and Sanctions Pressure
frictionVectors.details: The oil pipeline and associated fields are advancing with Chinese and regional backing, but Western environmental, sanctions, and reputational pressure complicates financing and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Foreign-Controlled Extractive Infrastructure
frictionVectors.details: Large infrastructure and mining projects increase state capacity but also deepen reliance on external contractors, lenders, and commodity buyers.

frictionVectors.title: Critical Minerals Competition
frictionVectors.details: Zambia is using competition among Chinese, Western, and Gulf investors to seek greater value capture from copper and cobalt, while retaining limited bargaining power over technology and processing.

frictionVectors.title: Power and Rail Bottlenecks
frictionVectors.details: Electricity shortages and unreliable export corridors constrain mining expansion and leave Zambia dependent on regional grids, transport links, and external infrastructure finance.

frictionVectors.title: Lithium and Platinum Ownership Tensions
frictionVectors.details: Export controls and beneficiation demands aim to increase domestic capture of mineral wealth, but Chinese and other foreign investors retain substantial influence over capital, processing, and market access.

frictionVectors.title: Currency and Sanctions Vulnerability
frictionVectors.details: Currency instability, sanctions, and restricted access to international finance raise the cost of infrastructure and force reliance on opaque bilateral and commodity-backed arrangements.
